samples.hyp: Estimating the SARS-CoV-2 testing requirements for preventing outbreaks in Lusaka Province, Zambia, focusing on asymptomatic individuals:
A longitudinal cohort study

The Coronavirus disease (COVID-19), caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), in Africa is characterized by a high proportion of asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic infections that contribute to the spread of the disease.
The prevalence and incidence of asymptomatic infection are not well understood.
However, research shows that addressing this disease is crucial for preventing the spread of SARS-CoV-2.

We developed a deterministic susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) epidemiological model to assess the impact of asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infections and to inform control strategies for the Lusaka Province in Zambia.
We modeled two scenarios; (1) assuming that asymptomatic individuals constituted 70% of all COVID-19 cases and (2) assuming that asymptomatic individuals constituted 50% of all COVID-19 cases.

For the sake of comparison, the model assumes that both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals are infectious, and secondly, and more importantly, that the infectiousness of asymptomatic individuals is a fraction of that of symptomatic individuals.

Assuming 70% of infected individuals are asymptomatic, daily universal testing at a rate of ≥7911 tests per 100,000 population would be sufficient to prevent the spread of asymptomatic individuals as a proportion of those infected.  However, if a similar rate of infection were to occur, a testing rate of ≥10028 tests per 100,000 population would be required.

In 50% of asymptomatic individuals, the subsequent lower incidence rate observed in the combined cohort of ≥ 4540 per 100,000 tested was sufficient to prevent disease progression to the two subsequent stages of disease spread among asymptomatic individuals compared to those who were symptomatic.
Discussion and consultation

Our model predicts that screening the entire population, including asymptomatic individuals, for COVID-19 could be a useful strategy for preventing the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Lusaka, Zambia, but it would be costly to implement.
Comprehensive testing in large cities like Lusaka could reduce the spread of COVID-19, but is it feasible?

In 2020, computer simulations suggested that an effective way to prevent the spread of COVID-19 in large populations could be achieved through universal testing, followed by isolation of those found to be infected.
However, the researchers stated that this method may be too expensive and impractical.
In the early stages of the pandemic, many people infected with COVID-19 were asymptomatic yet still infectious to others.
One study showed that 50% to 80% of people with COVID-19 were asymptomatic and may be responsible for 40% to 70% of onward transmission.
Researchers wanted to determine whether identifying and isolating asymptomatic individuals could help prevent the spread of COVID-19.
Similarly, they wanted to determine whether population screening, meaning testing people regardless of symptoms, helps to identify asymptomatic individuals.
Researchers developed a computer simulation showing how individuals transition between susceptible, infected, and recovered states.
The findings are based on data collected in the Lusaka Corridor in Zambia, a region that includes a major international airport located on the border between two countries.

Because COVID-19 symptoms varied from place to place, they examined four scenarios, in which 50% or 70% of COVID-19 patients were asymptomatic, and these asymptomatic patients were either highly infectious or had an intermediate infectiousness compared to symptomatic patients.
The research team found that it was possible to prevent the spread of COVID-19 by conducting mass testing and isolating all individuals who tested positive, even if they were asymptomatic.
It was estimated that to reduce the high infection rate of over 90% across all settings, 10% of the population in Lusaka needed to be vaccinated daily.
They also found that to maintain a constant number of COVID-19 cases, 22% of the population would need to be tested daily.
However, Zambia implemented measures to control the COVID-19 pandemic, and cases appeared to increase.
Mass testing reduced COVID-19 cases by 90% in a small Italian town.
However, no research has been conducted to show that it can work elsewhere in a large city.

This study suggests that researchers did not conduct a universal screening; however, they established a model indicating that universal screening could help prevent the spread of COVID-19 in large cities.
However, they cautioned that the method appears to be very expensive.
They also stated that this measure should be implemented alongside other measures such as lockdowns, contact tracing, and vaccination.
Zambian researchers also suggested that asymptomatic COVID-19 cases appeared to be more prevalent in Africa at that time.
Inferring the low prevalence of specific mutations in African populations due to variations in genomes and regions.
African populations are vastly underrepresented in genomic research despite harboring the highest genomic diversity and experiencing significant population movements across the globe.

Because time-series analysis of genomic surveillance data was not available for previous waves, we counted the frequency of different genomic variants to obtain polygenic risk scores (PRS) in a meta-analysis conducted across Africa and in datasets from South Africa, Uganda, and the UK to better understand the overall predictive power of the genomic surveillance studies.
The accuracy of PRS increases as more diverse groups are included in the study to represent a wider range of ancestries.
Among South African participants of diverse ethnicities and nationalities, we found that PRS prevalence was low across all ancestries but varied across different groups.
Differences in human genetic diversity in Africa contribute significantly more to the accuracy of PRS than the variation observed in other populations considered, such as those in the UK and Uganda.

We assessed the polygenic risk score (PRS) for sickle cell disease in the African population using a European-only reference panel and compared it with a diverse ancestry reference panel; increased diversity yielded higher prediction accuracy for hemoglobin levels and immune traits, indicating that a broader ancestry representation in the reference panel is needed to account for the diverse genetic architecture underlying sickle cell disease and its complications.
Differences in the accuracy of PRS across African populations from different regions compared to populations outside of Africa necessitate population-specific adjustments.
The reasons why we cannot accurately predict the prevalence of diseases in people of African descent.
Researchers say that the algorithm used to predict whether someone will develop a genetic disease is not accurate for people of African descent.
This is because the reference panel used for such predictions is largely representative of individuals of European ancestry.
GWAS studies investigate the relationship between genetic variations and diseases, and scientists use them to identify genes associated with diseases.
It is true that they use GWAS to calculate a person's susceptibility to disease or illness based on their genome.
However, the majority of genomic data in GWAS comes from people of European descent.
In this study, the researchers sought to evaluate the performance of a polygenic risk score (PRS) for predicting the risk of complex diseases using GWAS data from individuals of African ancestry.
Furthermore, they wanted to see if the GWAS, which includes a large number of African genomes, could improve the predictions made.
The measure is scientifically known as a “polygenic risk score”, or PRS.

They used a computer to calculate the predicted risk of developing sickle cell disease in Africans using GWAS, and also used African patient records to investigate certain traits or diseases that may result from genomic variations.
Using a European GWAS, they found that the genetic risk score for developing type 2 diabetes was higher in individuals of European ancestry compared to those of African ancestry.
They report that the prevalence of the disease is lower in African populations due to strong population immunity, a phenomenon contrasting with that observed in European populations.
They further stated that PRS accuracy increases as the African ancestry of the sample decreases.
Ethiopians had higher expectations of the disease outcome given their strong genetic similarity to Europeans.
When a GWAS incorporating a diverse African population was used, the accuracy of predictions increased.
The prevalence of blood-borne diseases was significantly higher.

Previous research has shown that PRS is lower in people of African ancestry, meaning that the GWAS approach produces underestimates of the risk of developing complex diseases for people of African descent.
But we know that this is not true.

This study shows that the low heritability of complex diseases is due to the fact that African genomes are poorly represented in GWAS datasets, meaning that current PRS scores are not helpful in predicting complex diseases in Africa.
Researchers suggest that it would be beneficial to use a reference panel that includes genomic data from individuals of African descent.
Therefore, further work is needed to expand GWAS to include a representative sample of people of African descent to better understand the genetic risk of complex diseases in Africans.
The researchers for this study were from Africa, the USA, and the UK.
A Study of the Use of Eye and Brick Examinations in the Management of Childhood Injuries and Childhood Eye Trauma in Namibia
About 851,340 women in Namibia are at risk of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, which can cause cervical cancer.
Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) combined with cryotherapy was confirmed as highly effective.
However, there was no message regarding the results of the children's oral swab tests.
This study investigated the effectiveness of visual and tactile assessments in diagnosing childhood injuries and oral lesions in Namibian children.
Findings showed that women with HPV, cervicitis, koilocytosis, and atypia are at a significantly increased risk of being detected by VIA.
Older women, especially those with HIV, are at a significantly increased risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
Visual inspection appears to perform well, however, the use of colposcopy in the follow-up of patients in Namibia should be evaluated in those found to have HR-HPV.
They support screening programs that include HPV testing in different age groups and in high-risk populations (e.g., those with HIV, immunosuppressive conditions).
Evaluation engagement can be strengthened by incorporating a framework that utilizes past evaluation findings, women's health goals, new communication strategies, and context-specific adaptations.
Women in Namibia at risk of cervical cancer should be screened and treated early.
Many screening methods can detect cervical cancer in women, but these methods are not routinely used in Namibia.
Researchers say that early screening and detection of early warning signs can save women from this deadly disease.
Cervical cancer affects many women worldwide.
One of the leading causes of childhood mouth cancer is the Human Papillomavirus, or HPV.
HPV is a virus that infects the cells of the cervix, causing lesions that can later develop into cancer.
Although HPV vaccines are available, many women in African countries, including Namibia, cannot access them.
This means that screening for the virus or its lesions is very beneficial for these women, as it is the best way to help prevent cervical cancer.
Researchers in this study suggest that hospitals therefore require appropriate guidelines and messaging regarding best practices for testing.
Furthermore, healthcare providers also need to know more about how factors such as age and lifestyle may increase a woman's risk of developing HPV and cervical cancer.
Consider the methods of some of the tests used to detect HPV and lesions.
They also wanted to compare examinations, for example, taking biopsies from children to examine whether there was any comparable damage and to look for lesions.
They also wanted to determine whether differences in women's age or the presence of other diseases such as HIV affected their risk of HPV and cervical cancer.
Understanding this message can help hospitals and clinics to better utilize diagnostic procedures.
Researchers reviewed the medical records of 214 women diagnosed and treated for HPV, genital warts, and cervical cancer at a hospital in Windhoek, Namibia.
Emphasis was placed on early childhood intervention, where this disease is most treatable.
They also collected data on women's ages and their overall health status.
In analyzing these records, they found that different tests provided clinicians with different messages, and that they could be very useful whether or not HPV had progressed to cancer.
For example, collaboration was highly valued in the collection and analysis of children's drawings.
However, lesions were predominantly detected by visual inspection using a method called “visual inspection with acetic acid” (VIA).
The advantage of this method is that it allows doctors to detect injuries quickly and non-invasively.
This is because it uses readily available, common gynecological examination instruments, such as a speculum (an instrument used to examine the vagina).
They also found that combining different methods provided doctors with more frequent messages about the risk of maternal mortality, especially after multiple examinations.
Furthermore, researchers found that older women, especially those with HIV, were more likely to be diagnosed with cervical cancer, therefore, screening them more frequently is crucial.
Researchers added that very few women were screened for HPV (without prior lesion detection) despite the availability of screening.
This could be a good way to quickly detect this disease.

In summary, they stated that their findings highlighted the need for a Namibian healthcare strategy to better coordinate HPV and childhood oral cancer prevention programs, using non-invasive and highly sensitive diagnostic methods.
This research was conducted by scientists from Namibia in collaboration with those from South Africa.
Treatment outcomes for people with both HBV and HIV compared to those with HBV alone in a South African population.

As part of the global effort to eliminate Hepatitis B virus (HBV), we aimed to characterize the differences between individuals with HBV monoinfection and those with HBV/HIV coinfection, to assess treatment response and to explore strategies for treatment optimization.
We present findings from a cohort of 115 adult patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) at a university hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
Thirty-nine (34%) of the participants were HIV and HBV co-infected.
We documented the clinical, epidemiological, and laboratory findings.

Compared to people with both HIV and HBV, those with HBV alone were less likely to have HBeAg (p=0.01), less likely to have cirrhosis (p<0.0001), and less likely to be on antiviral medication (p<0.0001); they were more likely to have detectable HBV DNA (p=0.04), and more likely to have clinical features of liver disease including mild/moderate thrombocytopenia (p=0.007), elevated bilirubin (p=0.004), and elevated APRI (p=0.02).
Three individuals developed hepatocellular carcinoma, all solely attributable to HBV infection.

Our findings confirm that individuals with HBV alone may experience greater challenges than those with both HIV and HBV, suggesting potential disparities in access to specialized healthcare facilities, monitoring, and treatment.
Researchers show what needs to be done to improve hepatitis B treatment.
In this recent study, researchers were able to demonstrate how co-infection with HBV and HIV may facilitate treatment compared to HBV mono-infection.
In sub-Saharan Africa, co-infection with HBV and HIV is a significant challenge.
Doctors need to understand the interaction between this virus and the drugs used to treat it in order to properly diagnose and treat patients.
Researchers wanted to compare treatment outcomes in patients with HBV alone and in patients with both HBV and HIV.
This study included 115 adult patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB).
They were recruited at Tygerberg Hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
Some patients had HIV (39), while others had only HBV.
Researchers examined color, age, and size, and conducted different in vitro and in vivo assays.
They found that patients with HBV alone had a lower expectation of receiving antiretroviral therapy, showing signs of liver disease (because HBV is a factor that can lead to severe liver disease).

Researchers were able to show that individuals with HBV alone had worse outcomes compared to those with both HIV and HBV, because individuals with both viruses were expected to be on antiretroviral therapy for HIV, which can also treat HBV.

This research shows the potential impact of differences in the provision of enhanced healthcare services, monitoring, and treatment for those with HBV when compared to those with HIV and HBV, with those having HIV and HBV benefiting more.
Researchers showed that we need to carefully monitor and manage patients with HBV monoinfection.
One of the limitations of this study was the small sample size, as the research was conducted in only one country and its healthcare system.
Some high-quality hospital practices may show results contrary to those found in this study.
Further research is needed to fully explore the differences observed in this study.
This paper highlights the strength of collaboration, with researchers from South Africa and the United Kingdom contributing to this project.
Using participants from South Africa in this research is beneficial to the African population.
Furthermore, this research could help in developing better treatments for people with HBV, HIV, or both.
Assessing the Impact of Gender Inequality on Women's Business Activities in the Local Government Area of Shiroro, Niger State

This research investigates the challenges and strategies employed by women entrepreneurs in the Local Government Area of Shiroro, Niger State, focusing specifically on women's access to finance, business establishment processes, and the challenges they face in establishing businesses.

A sample of 377 women was studied, and the results showed that women in Shiroro are predominantly entrepreneurs and are largely self-reliant financially, mostly engaging in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

The research also found that although vulnerability affects women entrepreneurs in terms of loss or reduction of start-up capital and similar challenges, the number of women starting businesses has not significantly decreased.

The research recommends that sustainable strategies to improve women's access to and utilization of financial services should be implemented, and that community-based monitoring mechanisms should be established and strengthened to prevent regional disparities.
Female entrepreneurs in Niger need more protection.
Researchers found that female entrepreneurs in Niger are highly resilient and resourceful, but access to justice remains a significant challenge.

Researchers sought to determine the extent to which female entrepreneurs in the Local Government Area of Shiroro, Niger State experience insecurity, and how this insecurity affects their businesses and financial well-being.
377 women in that area were asked about the challenges they faced in starting their businesses, financial planning, and instability.
They reported that 43% of women said they did not rely on men for financial support, while 32% said they had other people they relied on for financial support.
Researchers also found that 85% of the women earned income from various businesses, while a small minority reported relying on salaries.
About 56% earned income from agriculture, while another 79% obtained income from agriculture.
About one in five women earned income from weaving mats, brewing beer, making crafts, or washing clothes.
The majority of women (91%) reported to researchers that their businesses were affected by fear of robbery and crime.
They lost money along with their husbands in that robbery, and sometimes this forces them to care for their children without any support.
Those women also reported a lack of sufficient capital to expand their businesses.
Researchers reported that despite these challenges, women in Niger continue to perform well in their businesses.
They stated that the Shiroro area comprised people of diverse ethnicities and religions, and that this was beneficial for business.
This research challenges findings from other researchers who suggested that women have fewer business successes because they are primarily responsible for household duties.
However, these researchers say that the success of women entrepreneurs in this region of Niger is often hampered by theft and robbery.
Researchers emphasized that all stakeholders must collaborate to overcome all challenges that could hinder business success.
For example, women in Niger need access to more income, larger farms, and greater security.
They also agreed that women in business could form groups that could help them fight against thieves and criminals.
The effects of micronutrients including Selenium, Copper and Zinc during pregnancy on preterm birth: A study conducted in Malawi.
Giving birth to a preterm baby, that is, before 37 weeks of gestation.
Research was conducted to investigate the relationship between selenium, copper, and zinc, and preterm birth.
This study included 181 women, of whom 90/181 (49.7%) had given birth to term infants and 91/181 (50.3%) had given birth to preterm infants.

The selenium level in the blood was 77.0; SD 19.4µg/L, the chromium level was 2.50; SD 0.52 mg/L, and the zinc level was 0.77; SD 0.20 mg/L.  The reference ranges were 47-142µg/L, 0.76-1.59mg/L, and 0.59-1.11 mg/L, respectively.
The results show that there was no selenium or zinc deficiency, and high levels of iron in the blood of pregnant women.
Preterm birth is associated with low maternal zinc levels.
Zinc, copper and selenium deficiencies are associated with preterm birth.
Researchers found high levels of selenium, iron, and zinc in pregnant women who had not yet given birth, but it is not yet known whether these high levels are due to their diet.
Preterm birth occurs when a woman gives birth before 37 weeks of pregnancy.
Preterm birth leads to adverse health outcomes for the child, including birth defects and death.
Preterm birth can be caused by various factors, but the role of environmental and dietary exposures is not well understood.
These nutrients are beneficial for child development, but researchers want to know what happens if they are excessive.

In this study, researchers aimed to measure the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc in women who had given birth to preterm infants, to determine whether excess levels of any of these nutrients contributed to preterm birth.
Researchers collected blood samples from 181 women who delivered at two hospitals in Lilongwe, the capital city of Malawi, between June 2016 and March 2017.
Blood samples were analyzed in Norway for selenium, copper, and zinc concentrations.
About half of the 181 women in the study were mothers of young children, and researchers found significantly higher levels of selenium, iron, and zinc.
Then they adjusted their calculations to consider other factors such as age, socioeconomic status, and pregnancy history to confirm that these exposures lead to preterm births.
They concluded that high selenium and iron levels were not significantly associated with preterm birth, but that high zinc levels increased the odds of preterm birth more than sixfold.
However, the high threshold value was considered by researchers due to the toxicity of known inhibitors.

Having only 181 women participate in the study limited the researchers' ability to fully explore the challenges associated with high selenium levels, as a sample size of at least 600 would have been preferable.
The daily diet of the participants was not analyzed to determine the three sources of these nutrients, and neither height nor weight was recorded.
This is the first study to measure selenium, copper and zinc levels in pregnant women in Malawi.
Africa has the highest proportion of adolescent pregnancies – 18% and above compared to 5% in East Asia, therefore researchers wanted to find out whether diet plays a role.
Home range, site fidelity, and habitat use of the pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya
Animals have instincts to return to places and follow schedules that aid their survival.
Understanding such cultural practices is crucial for the conservation and management, especially of endangered species.
In this study, we tested the homing ability of the Pancake termite when displaced and investigated the influence of distance and habitat on homing success in Kitui County, Kenya.
Thirty-nine different bat species from twelve different caves were monitored from July 2020 to June 2022 using radio tracking, camera trapping, and observational data collection and analysis.
Fourteen families were relocated and their original homes and surrounding areas were surveyed.

Except for only two nests that successfully relocated to new locations, all other nests attempted to return to their original sites, with 46.15% following the exact same route back to their original nests and 15.38% reaching locations considered close to their original nests.
The high rate of re-infection clearly indicates that this is a highly re-infective strain.

Analysis of parasite prevalence in the reservoir showed no significant difference between the mean parasite prevalence in the reservoir and the overall mean prevalence over the 162 days monitored (F(1,22) = 0.0699, P >0.05), further confirming the resilience of this species.
Furthermore, observations during camera trapping revealed that pancake tortoises defend their territories, with males particularly aggressive towards other males attempting to intrude.
Defective pancake cells have enhanced ‘homing’ capabilities.

Researchers conducted a fascinating study on the East African pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri): the animals can find their way back home after being displaced a considerable distance from their original location.
Understanding the methods and reasons behind this practice may be crucial in conserving these endangered species.
The habit of discovering nests in these habitats appears to be very important for these cryptic species.
The ability to return to the same locations allows these animals to readily access food, find mates, and maintain territories; all of which increase their chances of survival and reproduction.
Although homing behaviour has been studied in marine and freshwater fish, researchers in this study say that little is known about the homing behaviour of anadromous fish.
In this study, researchers sought to understand the ecology of pancake tortoises in their natural habitats within the arid and semi-arid regions of Kenya.
Observe the animals as they moved and fed, and how they went to rest in the bushes or in the hollows of the trees.
Researchers have been observing groups of pancake tortoises for almost two years, and have set up cameras to record videos of them, although these were not visible.
Similarly, they placed the radio transmitter on frequency 14.
This small device allows researchers to track animal movements, including monitoring their daytime and nighttime locations.
The researchers then took some of the observed nests and relocated them to optimize their arrangement.
However, what surprised the researchers was this: two of the outbreaks started spreading from their origins, a distance of between 1 and 2.5 kilometers.
This led researchers to attempt removing the parasites from their location to see if they would exhibit the same ‘homing’ behavior.
Surprisingly, nearly half of the released ants were able to find their way back to their nests in unfamiliar terrain, traveling over 1.5 kilometers.
The remaining 15% of the fragments could be mapped back to a single region, but their precise origin could not be determined.
Researchers also found that different species had almost the same home range size, indicating that the species tend to use the same areas for resting.
Camera trap images showed that male primates were defending territories, meaning they were able to fight off other males that attempted to encroach on their territories or females.

Researchers stated that this was the first time observing the homing behavior of pancake tortoises, and that the results showed these tortoises prefer to rest and remain in specific locations whenever possible.
Their research does not explain how the bats found their way back home, therefore, future research should focus on understanding this crucial aspect.
Because animals sometimes need to be moved to a new location for conservation purposes, this message can help wildlife managers maintain healthy populations in their existing habitats.
This research was conducted in collaboration between scientists from Kenya and China, and adds to our understanding of homing behavior in bats and other animals.
The pharmacokinetics of high-dose rifampicin administered intravenously were compared with those administered intrathecally in patients with tuberculous meningitis:
Exploratory Data Analysis
High doses of rifampicin administered intravenously can improve outcomes in tuberculous meningitis but cannot be administered in high-density settings.

We hypothesized that the rifampicin concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid would be similar between an oral dose of 35 mg/kg body weight and an intravenous dose of mg/kg, as these were used in the pharmacokinetic study of the drug in tuberculous meningitis.
We conducted a randomized controlled trial to assess the efficacy of high-dose anti-tuberculosis medication in the treatment of tuberculous meningitis.
HIV-positive patients with tuberculous meningitis were recruited from South African hospitals and randomly assigned to three different rifampicin dosage groups.
Standard (oral 10 mg/kg), high (oral 35 mg/kg), and intravenous (20 mg/kg).
High-quality samples were obtained on day 3.
The results were analyzed using noncompartmental analysis, and drug exposure was compared using geometric mean ratios (GMRs).
Sixty-four participants were sampled for drug administration (standard dose, n = 17; high oral dose, n = 15; intramuscular dose, n = 14).
The median CD4 count was 130 cells/mm3 (interquartile range [IQR], 66 to 253 cells/mm3).

The geometric mean area under the rifampicin concentration-time curve from 0 to 24 h (AUC0–24) was 42.9 mg·h/ml (95% confidence interval [CI], 24.5 to 75.0 mg·h/ml) for the standard dose, 295.2 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 189.9 to 458.8 mg·h/ml) for the high oral dose, and 206.5 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 154.6 to 275.8 mg·h/ml) for the intravenous dose.

The AUC0–24 GMR for rifampicin was 1.44 (90% CI, 0.84 to 2.21), while the maximum observed plasma concentration (Cmax) GMR was 0.89 (90% CI, 0.63 to 1.23) for the higher oral dose compared to the intravenous dose.
The AUC0–24 of rifampicin in plasma was higher after a 35-mg/kg oral dose than after a 20-mg/kg intravenous dose during the initial days of tuberculosis (TB) treatment.
Findings support the use of oral rifampicin in the treatment of tuberculous meningitis in a prospective study.
Higher doses of the drug can be tested on HIV patients with TB meningitis.
Researchers confirmed that it is worthwhile to investigate whether higher doses of rifampicin can save HIV patients with tuberculous meningitis.
Three out of five HIV-positive patients who develop tuberculous meningitis die from this life-threatening disease.
Survivors often experience long-term damage to the nervous system and cognitive impairment.
This can affect their thoughts and behavior.
Some patients experience numbness or tingling, or numbness in parts of the face or body.
Rifampicin, a potent antibacterial drug used to treat tuberculosis, is often administered intravenously in an attempt to kill the bacteria causing tuberculous meningitis.
Severely ill patients often have difficulty swallowing these pills.
Rifampicin can also be administered intravenously.
The virus shed in the patient's saliva can be transmitted.
No pharmacokinetic studies were conducted to determine how the body absorbs this drug using this method.
Administering medication via intravenous infusion requires additional equipment, a bed, and a trained medical professional skilled in properly inserting the intravenous line.
Therefore, this is not something that can be done in underdeveloped regions.
Doctors know that rifampicin does not penetrate well into the cerebrospinal fluid, the brain, and the eye, where bacteria can hide.
This is why higher doses are needed to kill all the bacteria in the patient's body.
However, the researchers did not confirm how a higher dose might be effective and safe.

Therefore, South African and British researchers sought to determine, using a small number of patients, whether it is safe to administer high doses of rifampicin as a capsule or in syrup, and how their bodies would metabolize each dose.
This is important to note, as other researchers have not yet begun to conduct such trials, where they plan to administer higher doses of rifampicin to more patients.
One of three rifampicin regimens was given to 46 HIV-positive patients in South Africa with tuberculous meningitis.
The initial treatment was the standard capso drug regimen, providing 10mg of rifampicin per kilogram of patient weight.
Another group received a higher dose of 35 milligrams of capsaicin per kilogram of patient weight.
The third group received 20 milligrams per kilogram of patient weight.
Blood samples were collected from patients after three days.
Researchers measured the concentration of rifampicin in their blood plasma.
Higher rifampicin concentrations were found in the bodies of patients who received higher doses compared to those who received standard or lower doses.
The drug concentration in the serum was consistent with the oral dose.
That drug was more effective in patients who received a higher dose than those who received only the standard dose.
According to the researchers, this indicates that the survival of patients with tuberculous meningitis can improve if they receive adequate doses of rifampicin.
It doesn't matter whether they received the vaccine as a single dose or in multiple doses – the important thing is that they received the free doses, because now their bodies can produce antibodies.
The results support those from studies conducted in Uganda and Indonesia.

For example, two small trials conducted in Indonesia showed that the lives of many patients with multi-drug resistant tuberculosis could be saved if they were given high doses of rifampicin orally or intravenously.
However, the researchers caution that the participants in this study were not representative of the target population, which may affect the findings.
The research was conducted in South Africa.
Supporting a plan to conduct a trial to assess whether administering higher doses of rifampicin is beneficial for HIV patients with tuberculous meningitis.
It is hoped that this type of treatment will save the lives of other people in Africa and other parts of the world where tuberculous meningitis is a significant problem.
Can the use of seaweed and other organic matter improve the quality of coastal wetland soil?
Soil erosion is a major constraint to agriculture in sub-Saharan Africa.
Many authors have highlighted the benefits of using compost and manure in soil improvement.

In this study, a 30-day feeding trial was conducted using 120 g feed rations.  The rations consisted of  a mixture of  insect frass,  rice husk ash,  coconut shell ash (coco300 and coco700), or a composite feed made from insect frass; and a composite feed of rice husk ash or insect frass, each supplemented with 1% cococomp and soil.

Further analyses included incubation studies using different combinations of earthworms and litter (1% earthworm + 1% litter: 1% soil) to investigate their effects on soil aggregation, soil pH, soil organic carbon derived from microorganisms, total nitrogen, and available nitrogen.
Both compost and vermicompost, whether used alone or in combination with vermicompost, increased soil pH by 0.28-2.29 units compared to the untreated control.

The initial release from single-source/clustered aerosol/droplet emissions or a combination of aerosol and droplet sources was higher than non-clustered sources, similar to that from droplet sources alone.
Carbon sequestration in the fertilized and unfertilized plots increased by 37% and 117%, respectively, compared to the control.
The addition of both compost and manure increased soil microbial biomass by 132%, while the addition of manure alone increased it by 247% compared to the control (no amendment).

In summary, the research showed that the application of compost and biochar, either individually or in combination, improved soil quality indicators such as soil pH and soil microbial biomass, and enhanced soil carbon sequestration by increasing carbon storage and reducing soil carbon loss, depending on the amount of carbon dioxide released from the soil.
Soil texture and structure influence crop yield.
This research investigates how biochar, a carbon-rich material produced from plant biomass, can be used to improve soil quality in sub-Saharan Africa.
Research found that compost improves soil quality similarly to other methods that can be used (which are expensive and not readily available).
One of the biggest challenges in agriculture in sub-Saharan Africa is land scarcity.
Very good soil quality can lead to high crop yields, which can reduce rural poverty and prevent environmental degradation.
Research shows that biochar, which contains carbon, can be used to improve soil fertility.
Incomplete combustion of carbon-containing materials or plants in the presence of limited or no oxygen produces smoke.
Studies have shown that cover crops increase soil organic matter, improve water and air infiltration, and enhance soil microbial activity.
This research investigated how the use of mulch and compost affects soil quality.  Indicators such as soil texture, soil pH, microbial activity, carbon content, and nitrogen gas emissions were used.
Researchers performed pyrolysis of wood chips, sawdust, and rice husk at 450 °C in an oxygen-free environment.
Researchers conducted experiments using clay samples, firing them at temperatures ranging from 300 °C to 700 °C.
Researchers then incubated the selected soil samples amended with the amendments for 30 days.

The criteria for defining critical illness included a high risk of imminent death; failure of vital organ systems; the need for intensive care to prevent death; and the potential for recovery.

The challenges in explaining effective treatment included the detection, monitoring, and treatment of severe illness; support for essential services; primary and specialized care; all aspects of severe illness management; and expert clinicians and specialized equipment.
Our agreed definition of critical illness is, “a medical condition characterized by organ dysfunction, a high risk of imminent death if treatment is not provided, and the potential for recovery”.
Our agreed-upon definition of intensive care is, “to identify, monitor, and treat critically ill patients through the initiation and escalation of support for vital organ systems.”
The concepts of severe illness and intensive care are not clearly defined and are used in various ways.

Through a review of usage and interpretation in literature and with experts, we have identified challenges in interpreting these concepts and propose interpretations that can aid in application, research, and policy development.
